one_liner: Classic CPU OCR engine (LSTM line recognizer); with one process per core it out-throughputs single-stream GPU EasyOCR.
what_it_does: Tesseract turns page images into text (plain text, hOCR, PDF, TSV, ALTO, PAGE) using an LSTM line recognizer plus the legacy Tesseract 3 pattern engine, with traineddata models for over 100 languages. It ships as libtesseract (C API capi.h and C++ API baseapi.h) and the tesseract command-line program; Python users usually reach it through pytesseract, which is what the benchmark did. It is not a drop-in for EasyOCR: different API, different models, and no GPU path.
how_it_is_fast: The LSTM forward pass runs on 8-bit integer weights through SIMD matrix-vector kernels (IntSimdMatrix: AVX2, SSE, NEON and RVV variants) and float dot products (AVX, AVX-512F, FMA, SSE, NEON), picked at runtime by simddetect.cpp (the dotproduct variable defaults to auto). The CMake build uses float rather than double for the LSTM by default (FAST_FLOAT ON). The measured win over EasyOCR comes mostly from the deployment pattern, not the kernels: one single-threaded Tesseract process per page across every vCPU (OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=1), which is the batch setup Tesseract's FAQ recommends, against EasyOCR reading one page at a time on one GPU.
when_to_use: Bulk OCR of clean printed pages (books, reports) on CPU-only machines, run as one single-threaded process per core with OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=1
Historical printed books in German, French or English, where it scored 0.4-3.7% CER in the same leaderboard, close to large OCR VLMs
Deployments that cannot ship a GPU, PyTorch or a VLM runtime and need a small native C/C++ library with Apache-2.0 licensing
Pipelines that need word boxes or hOCR/ALTO/PDF text layers rather than Markdown
when_not_to_use: Handwriting: 56.1% CER on the IAM handwriting track, against 2.0% for dots.mocr
Noisy, rotated or phone-photo scans: on the stress ladder CER jumps to 55.5% under noise and 81.9% at 8 degrees of rotation, and stress pages dominated its wall time
Multi-column layouts and tables: it reads in raster order and passed 0.0% of the olmOCR-bench table tests
Single-page interactive latency on a GPU box: GPU EasyOCR had a lower median per-track latency on G4, A100 and L4 in the same runs
Maximum CPU-or-GPU throughput: PaddleOCR 3 (4.13 pages/s) and PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 (5.84 pages/s) beat it on the same G4 runtime

integration.form: shared lib (libtesseract) plus CLI; static build possible
integration.dependencies: Leptonica 1.80 or newer (image I/O); optional libarchive and libcurl; per-language traineddata files (tessdata, tessdata_fast or tessdata_best)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (CMake 3.22+, switches to C++20 when the compiler supports it); autotools build also available
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 with runtime-dispatched SSE4.1, AVX, AVX2, FMA and AVX-512F kernels; ARM NEON; RISC-V RVV; generic fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: Not documented in the repository. The FAQ recommends one Tesseract process per CPU core with OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=1 for batch work; wrappers such as iText pdfOCR document one engine instance per thread; reusing one TessBaseAPI object across images can give inconsistent results unless ClearAdaptiveClassifier() is called

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the throughput numbers: each track (50-60 pages) is smaller than one Tesseract batch (2 x workers, 96 on G4), so each track is one parallel map whose wall time is set by the slowest page. The stress track alone took 44.9 of 62.0 s on G4 (stress 1.22 vs EasyOCR 1.26 pages/s, books 7.39 vs 0.69), 146.5 of 264.0 s on A100 and 70.4 of 94.1 s on the TPU host, so the headline pages/s mostly measures a few slow degraded pages (inferred from the per-track timing in status.json; per-page times are not recorded).

Not like-for-like: Tesseract ran 8 to 48 processes in parallel against EasyOCR's single stream, and the Tesseract latency pass timed only the first 8 pages per track while EasyOCR's latency covers every page. Each pytesseract call also starts a fresh process that reloads eng+fra+deu+lat, which inflates Tesseract's single-page latency.

Builds with OpenMP use up to four threads per page; running many processes without OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=1 oversubscribes cores (issue #1662 thread: removing OpenMP made one multithreaded app about 33% faster). CMake now defaults OPENMP_BUILD to OFF.

Speed depends heavily on the model set: tessdoc Benchmarks.md shows tessdata_best 6.20 s vs tessdata_fast 2.12 s on one image with 5.0.1, and 4.1.3 without AVX at 37.6 s, so a distro build or model choice can swing results several-fold.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No OCR entry is catalogued yet; the image-codecs siblings (libjpeg-turbo, QOI, fpng and others) decode or encode images rather than read text, so pick Tesseract only when the job is text extraction on CPU.
verified_claims_summary: In the single-author kvenanzi/ocr leaderboard (215-page standard profile, Google Colab), distro Tesseract 5.3.4 via pytesseract (LSTM, eng+fra+deu+lat, one process per page across all vCPUs) reached 3.47 pages/s on G4 (AMD EPYC 9B45, 48 vCPU) against 1.11 for EasyOCR 1.7.2 on the RTX PRO 6000 GPU, and 0.68-0.82 vs 0.34-0.49 on T4, L4 and A100, and 2.28 vs 0.20 on the TPU-v6e host CPU; compiler and build flags are not stated. Per track on G4 the win is books 7.39 vs 0.69 and docs 5.27 vs 0.66 pages/s, while EasyOCR is slightly faster on the stress track (1.26 vs 1.22).
status_note: Actively maintained (latest release 5.5.3, last commit 2026-10-10), Apache-2.0 and widely packaged, so copyable; the benchmarked 5.3.4 distro build is several releases behind current main.
